newsitem.title: UK: Political row causes Diana to scrap landmine talks.
newsitem.headline: Political row causes Diana to scrap landmine talks.

text.p: Princess Diana pulled out of a meeting at Britain's parliament on Wednesday with campaigners for a global ban on landmines, complaining that political controversy over her involvement made it "untenable" to attend.

Diana, ex-wife of heir to the throne Prince Charles, had been invited to a private meeting of the all-party Landmines Eradication Group, which hailed her agreement to visit the House of Commons as a major boost for its campaign.

But it ran into criticism from some members of the main opposition Conservative party who said she risked contravening an unwritten rule that members of the royal family must not intervene in political issues.
A statement issued by her office said Diana had made it clear that her involvement in the issues surrounding anti-personnel landmines was exclusively humanitarian.
"The evening's all-party private meeting was to have been an opportunity for the princess to be further briefed on certain of the issues.

"Details of the meeting have, however, now been made public and a political dimension has been introduced to its purpose. As a consequence the princess's attendance has been made untenable," the statement said.
It said the princess, who decided to pull out after returning from a visit to New York, had invited the organisers of Wednesday's meeting to brief her at a later date.
Diana, who toured war-ravaged Angola in January to meet landmine victims, has criticised countries which trade in landmines and has called for a worldwide ban.
Last month the new Labour government promised to destroy all Britain's anti-personnel mines by 2005, pursuing its pledge to put human rights at the centre of foreign policy.
In doing so, it adopted a tougher policy than the previous Conservative government of John Major.

"I'm sad she's not coming," said former BBC war correspondent Martin Bell, now an independent MP who is a member of the all-party landmines group. "I think she has no reason not to be here. This is not a political issue."
But Conservative MP Andrew Robathan said: "I think she was wisely advised not to come because I don't wish to see here being dragged into any sort of political dispute."
